OpenGL Texturing
▪ Texturing procedure
• Fetch interpolated texel value from texture
• Use texel value to modulate fragment color or depth
▪ Configuration
• Per texture
• Provide texture storage and data
• Configure texture filtering for minification and magnification
• Configure texture wrapping
• Generate mipmaps when mipmapped filters are used
• Per geometric object
• Associate texture coordinates with VAO
• Bind texture object to texture unit
• Set sampler uniform to texture unit

OpenGL Minification & Magnification 1/3
▪ OpenGL exposes two texture filtering parameters:
• GL_TEXTURE_MIN_FILTER
• GL_TEXTURE_MAG_FILTER
▪ Texture minification (GL_TEXTURE_MIN_FILTER) options
• GL_NEAREST - nearest neighbor interpolation
• GL_LINEAR - bilinear interpolation
• GL_NEAREST_MIPMAP_NEAREST - nearest neighbor mipmap interpolation
• GL_NEAREST_MIPMAP_LINEAR - linear interpolation of nearest neighbor mipmap interpolation
• GL_LINEAR_MIPMAP_NEAREST - bilinear mipmap interpolation
• GL_LINEAR_MIPMAP_LINEAR - trilinear mipmap interpolation
▪ Texture magnification (GL_TEXTURE_MAG_FILTER) options -GL_NEAREST - nearest neighbor
interpolation -GL_LINEAR - bilinear interpolation

Seiten-Metadaten: Bilder=1, Rechtecke=4, Kurven=0, Linien=0
Texture Wrapping 1/4
▪ Texture wrapping specifies border handling behavior when accessing texture outside the
[0, 1]D
normalized texture value range
▪ Texture wrapping mode is part of texture specification, and specified separately for each texture
dimension
▪ Two main modes exist
• Clamping: GL_CLAMP_TO_EDGE, GL_CLAMP_TO_BORDER
• Repetition: GL_REPEAT, GL_MIRRORED_REPEAT
Interactive Computer Graphics 19/07/2026 59
[Seite 61]
Seiten-Metadaten: Bilder=2, Rechtecke=4, Kurven=0, Linien=0
Texture Wrapping 2/4
▪ GL_CLAMP_TO_EDGE
• Texture coordinates below 0 become 0
• Texture coordinates above 1 become 1
• Results in constant continuation of texture
▪ GL_CLAMP_TO_BORDER
• Texture coordinates below 0 become 0
• Texture coordinates above 1 become 1
• Coordinates originally outside range mapped to definable border color
Interactive Computer Graphics 19/07/2026 60
[Seite 62]
Seiten-Metadaten: Bilder=1, Rechtecke=4, Kurven=0, Linien=0
Texture Wrapping 3/4
▪ GL_REPEAT
• Texture coordinates ignore digits before decimal point, and use digits after decimal point as
texture coordinates
• Results in periodic continuation of normalized texture space
▪ GL_MIRRORED_REPEAT
• Texture coordinates ignore digits before decimal point, and digits after decimal point are
subtracted from 1 in alternating manner before used as texture coordinates
• Results in periodic, mirrored continuation of normalized texture space

9.5 Normal Mapping
Encoding surface detail in texture space

Motivation
▪ Render content dichotomy
• Shape: Triangles are used to generate geometric details
k k k
• Appearance: Textures are used to generate material variations ( a , d , s )
▪ Consequences
• Surface details require large amounts of triangles (which would impact rendering performance)
• Material details captured by textures do not match geometric details captured by geometry

9.6 Environment Mapping
Sampling directional environment data for reflections and lighting
Visual Computing Group
Institute of Media Informatics
[Seite 84]
Seiten-Metadaten: Bilder=1, Rechtecke=4, Kurven=0, Linien=0
Environment Mapping Motivation
▪ Many reflective and glossy materials show light from their surroundings
▪ Explicitly tracing all reflection rays is expensive in interactive rendering
▪ Environment maps provide a compact representation of incident radiance
▪ Typical use cases
• mirror-like reflections
• glossy reflections
• skyboxes
• image-based lighting
Interactive Computer Graphics 19/07/2026 80
[Seite 85]
Seiten-Metadaten: Bilder=2, Rechtecke=4, Kurven=0, Linien=0
Environment Mapping Process
▪ Environment mapping simulates reflections by sampling an image of the surrounding scene
▪ The environment is treated as if it were infinitely far away
▪ The reflected view direction determines which part of the environment is visible
[Need for Speed no Limits]
Interactive Computer Graphics 19/07/2026 81
[Seite 86]
Seiten-Metadaten: Bilder=0, Rechtecke=4, Kurven=0, Linien=0
Environment Mapping Assumptions
▪ The environment is assumed to be far away
• translation of the object does not change the sampled environment
▪ The reflected object does not reflect itself
▪ Nearby dynamic objects are usually missing
▪ The approximation works best for
• distant surroundings
• small reflective objects
• moderately rough reflections
• visually complex environments

V N

R
▪ The resulting reflection vector is used to access the environment map
R
▪ is calculated analog to the Phong illumination model
R = 2 ⋅ (V ⋅ N ) ⋅ N − V
▪ In GLSL, this is usually computed per fragment

Environment Mapping Types 1/2
▪ Different parameterizations store directional data in different ways
▪ They differ with respect to
• distortion
• filtering behavior
• hardware support
• implementation complexity
Interactive Computer Graphics 19/07/2026 85
[Seite 90]
Seiten-Metadaten: Bilder=0, Rechtecke=4, Kurven=0, Linien=0
Environment Mapping Types 2/2
▪ Spherical environment maps
• compact representation in one 2D texture
• strong distortion near the border
• difficult filtering and interpolation behavior
▪ Dual-paraboloid maps
• avoid six cube faces
• introduce distortion and seam issues
• rarely used in modern teaching pipelines
▪ Cube maps
• better directional uniformity
• direct hardware support
• natural representation for skyboxes, reflections, and IBL
▪ In modern real-time rendering, cube maps are the standard representation!

Spherical Environment Mapping
▪ A sphere map stores the environment as seen in a perfectly reflective sphere
▪ It was useful before cube maps became widely supported in graphics hardware
▪ It is mainly relevant today as historical context
▪ Important limitations
• non-uniform distortion
• singularity at the outer border
• problematic linear interpolation
Interactive Computer Graphics 19/07/2026 89
[Seite 94]
Seiten-Metadaten: Bilder=1, Rechtecke=4, Kurven=0, Linien=0
Sphere Map Distortion
▪ Sphere-map texels represent differently sized regions of the environment
▪ Distortion is especially problematic in the outer region of the map
▪ Hardware performs linear texture filtering, not spherical interpolation
▪ For modern real-time graphics, this is one reason cube maps are preferred

Sphere Map Interpolation
▪ Sphere maps represent non-linear images
▪ Two sphere map texels should be interpolated along an arc
• Graphics hardware does not support spherical interpolation
• Interpolation in the inner area is little distorted
• Interpolation in the outer area is highly distorted
▪ arc interpolation
▪ linear interpolation

Cube Environment Mapping
▪ Cube maps are represented by 6 square textures forming the sides of a cube
▪ The cube is centered around the shading point or camera
▪ Each face stores the environment as seen through one side of the cube
▪ A 3D direction vector is used to select the face and lookup position

Cube Mapping Distortion
▪ Cube maps still distort the environment
▪ The distortion is distributed more uniformly than in sphere maps
▪ There are no pole singularities
▪ The main artifacts occur at cube-face boundaries

Sampling Direction
▪ A cube map is sampled with a 3D direction vector
▪ The largest absolute component of the direction selects the cube face
▪ The remaining two components determine the 2D position on that face
▪ For reflection mapping, use the reflected view vector

Practical Cube-Map Issues
▪ Cube-map reflections are an approximation
• environment is assumed to be far away
• object does not reflect itself
• other moving objects are usually missing
▪ Important implementation details
• use mipmaps for glossy / blurred reflections
• enable seamless cube-map filtering where available
• sample color maps in the correct color space
• use dynamic cube maps only when reflections must update

Chapter 9 - Texturing
Cube Mapping Pros and Cons
▪ Advantages
• direct hardware support
• limited distortion
• no pole singularities
• natural representation for directional data
• suitable for skyboxes, reflections, and IBL
▪ Disadvantages
• seams may occur at cube-face boundaries
• face orientation must be consistent
• filtering and compression can reveal edges
• local reflections are only approximate
Interactive Computer Graphics 19/07/2026 105
[Seite 111]
Seiten-Metadaten: Bilder=0, Rechtecke=4, Kurven=0, Linien=0
Spherical Environment Mapping Assumptions
▪ Environment assumed far from object to be textured
▪ Self-reflection not taken into account
• Object to be textured assumed a convex shape(even if it is not geometrically convex)
▪ No other moving objects in the environment
• Interreflection is not taken into account
▪ Object to be textured curved as much as possible
• Visually suppresses distortions
Interactive Computer Graphics 19/07/2026 106
[Seite 112]
Seiten-Metadaten: Bilder=0, Rechtecke=4, Kurven=0, Linien=0
Spherical Environment Mapping Conclusions
▪ Advantages
• Contains panoramic image of an environment in a single texture
• Filtering and LoD formation takes place within a single texture
▪ Disadvantages
• Singularity along the outer disc border
• Linear interpolation performed by graphics hardware
• Distortion and filtering problems increase in front half-space
• 2D texture memory is not fully utilized
• Generation of panoramic images not supported by graphics hardware

3D Texture as a Voxel Grid
▪ A 3D texture stores samples on a regular three-dimensional grid
▪ A sample is often called a voxel
▪ Each voxel can store scalar, vector, or multi-channel data
• Density, temperature, material ID
• Color and opacity
• Vector fields or simulation attributes
▪ The shader accesses the grid through normalized texture coordinates
3
(s, t, r) ∈ [0, 1]

Object Space to Texture Space
▪ 3D texture coordinates are usually derived from object-space position
▪ For a volume-aligned bounding box

max min
▪ A texture-coordinate transformation can translate, scale, or rotate the volume
▪ This makes the texture behave like material inside the object, not like a 2D decal on the surface

3D Texture Access
▪ For each fragment, texture coordinates are interpolated
▪ A 3D lookup fetches the neighboring voxel values
▪ Linear filtering in 3D performs trilinear interpolation

Seiten-Metadaten: Bilder=0, Rechtecke=4, Kurven=0, Linien=0
3D Mipmaps and Filtering
▪ 3D textures can use mipmaps analogously to 2D textures
▪ Each mip level halves width, height, and depth
k + 1 k
▪ Level contains one eighth of the voxels of level
▪ Useful for
• reducing aliasing during minification
• representing multi-scale volume detail
• accelerating coarse previews or LoD rendering
▪ Limitation
• mipmapping averages data values, which can change semantic meaning for labels or sparse
densities

Seiten-Metadaten: Bilder=2, Rechtecke=4, Kurven=0, Linien=0
Solid Texturing
▪ 3D textures can define material throughout the interior of an object
▪ Surface fragments sample the material at their 3D position
▪ This avoids seams caused by 2D UV unwrapping
▪ Useful for materials with volumetric structure
• wood grain
• marble
• stone
• noise-based procedural detail
Images adapted from [Kopf et al., SIGGRAPH 2007]

Seiten-Metadaten: Bilder=0, Rechtecke=4, Kurven=0, Linien=0
Volumetric Data as Texture Data
▪ Volume data is often represented as a scalar field
ρ = f (x, y, z)
▪ Examples
• CT or MRI intensity
• smoke density
• cloud water content
• scientific simulation values
▪ Store the scalar field in a 3D texture
▪ The shader converts sampled values into visual appearance
Interactive Computer Graphics 19/07/2026 117
[Seite 124]
Seiten-Metadaten: Bilder=0, Rechtecke=4, Kurven=0, Linien=0
Transfer Functions
▪ A transfer function maps data values to optical properties
T (ρ) = (c, α)
c
▪ Color emphasizes material classes or value ranges
α
▪ Opacity controls which structures become visible
▪ Common choices
→
• 1D transfer function: scalar value color and opacity
→
• 2D transfer function: value and gradient magnitude color and opacity
▪ Transfer-function design is often the central interaction in volume rendering
Interactive Computer Graphics 19/07/2026 118
[Seite 125]
Seiten-Metadaten: Bilder=2, Rechtecke=4, Kurven=0, Linien=0
Volume Rendering with 3D Textures
▪ 3D grid data is stored in a 3D texture
▪ Slice-based volume rendering draws proxy geometry through the volume
▪ Slices are usually orthogonal to the view direction
▪ Each slice samples the 3D texture and applies the transfer function
▪ Slices are blended back to front or front to back
Interactive Computer Graphics 19/07/2026 119
[Seite 126]
Seiten-Metadaten: Bilder=0, Rechtecke=4, Kurven=0, Linien=0
Front-to-Back Alpha Compositing
▪ Volume rendering approximates absorption and emission along a ray
c α
▪ For a sample with color i and opacity i
C = C + (1 − α ) ⋅ α ⋅ c
out in in i i
α = α + (1 − α ) ⋅ α
out in in i
▪ Front-to-back compositing enables early ray termination
▪ Stop when accumulated opacity is close to one
Interactive Computer Graphics 19/07/2026 120
[Seite 127]
Seiten-Metadaten: Bilder=0, Rechtecke=25, Kurven=2, Linien=0
Ray Marching Volume Rendering
▪ Instead of drawing slices, cast one ray per fragment through the volume
▪ Repeatedly sample the 3D texture along the ray
▪ Apply the transfer function at every sample
▪ Composite samples until the ray exits the volume or becomes opaque
1 for (float t = tEntry; t < tExit; t += stepSize) {
2 vec3 p = rayOrigin + t * rayDirection;
3 float rho = texture(volumeTex, p).r;
4 vec4 sample = texture(transferTex, rho);
5 color.rgb += (1.0 - color.a) * sample.a * sample.rgb;
6 color.a += (1.0 - color.a) * sample.a;
7 if (color.a > 0.98) break;
8 }

Gradients and Volume Lighting
▪ Gradients estimate local orientation in the scalar field
▪ Central differences approximate the gradient
ρ(x + Δ, y, z) − ρ(x − Δ, y, z)
⎡ ⎤
∇ρ ≈ ⎢ ρ(x, y + Δ, z) − ρ(x, y − Δ, z) ⎥
⎣ ⎦
ρ(x, y, z + Δ) − ρ(x, y, z − Δ)
▪ The normalized gradient can be used like a surface normal
▪ This enables Phong-like or physically based lighting effects inside the volume
Interactive Computer Graphics 19/07/2026 122
[Seite 129]
Seiten-Metadaten: Bilder=0, Rechtecke=4, Kurven=0, Linien=0
Quality and Performance Trade-Offs
▪ Step size
• smaller steps improve quality but increase cost
• larger steps are faster but can miss thin structures
▪ Opacity correction
• keeps appearance stable when step size changes
▪ Acceleration
• early ray termination
• empty-space skipping
• bricking and paging for large volumes
• lower-resolution mip levels for previews
▪ Main trade-off: image quality versus samples per ray
Interactive Computer Graphics 19/07/2026 123
[Seite 130]
Seiten-Metadaten: Bilder=0, Rechtecke=4, Kurven=0, Linien=0
3D Texturing Takeaways
▪ 3D textures generalize 2D texture lookup from surfaces to volumes
▪ They are useful for solid materials, volumetric effects, and sampled scientific data
▪ Trilinear interpolation provides smooth access to voxel grids
▪ Volume rendering turns sampled data into color and opacity along viewing rays
▪ Transfer functions and compositing determine what becomes visible
▪ Performance is dominated by memory footprint and number of samples
Interactive Computer Graphics 19/07/2026 124
[Seite 131]
Seiten-Metadaten: Bilder=0, Rechtecke=4, Kurven=0, Linien=0
Chapter Summary
▪ Textures are sampled GPU data sources used by shaders
• Color, opacity, normals, roughness, height, masks, and volume density
▪ Texture coordinates define where texture data is sampled
(s, t, r)
• UV mapping, texture transformations, and 3D coordinates
▪ Texture formats, channel semantics, and color space determine correct interpretation
• Color textures use sRGB decoding; data textures stay linear
▪ Filtering, mipmapping, and anisotropy control reconstruction quality
• They reduce aliasing during magnification and minification
▪ Specialized texture mappings add appearance detail without adding geometry
• Normal mapping, environment mapping, material texture stacks
▪ 3D textures extend texturing from surfaces to volumes
• Voxels, transfer functions, ray marching, compositing, and gradients

• Shadow-casting scene objects(Occluder)

Umbra and Penumbra
▪ Point light sources
• Result in hard shadows
• High intensity contrast between shadowed andnon-shadowed region
▪ Area light sources
• Result in soft shadows
• Core shadow (umbra): area completely occluded wrt. light source
• Penumbra (Penumbra): area only partially occludedwrt. light source
▪ Size of shadow region depends on
• Area of light source
• Distance of light source to scene object

Chapter 10 - Shadows
Observations 1/2
▪ Possible shadow generation approaches
• Shadows as surfaces: exploit hidden-surface algorithms
• Shadows as projection: create shadows from A to Bby projecting A onto B from light source
▪ Static vs. dynamic scenes
• Shadows are static in scenes with static lighting and scene objects (shadow computation
possible as preprocess)
• Shadows are dynamic in scenes with dynamic lighting and/ordynamic scene objects(shadows
must be computed per frame)
Interactive Computer Graphics 09/07/2026 13
[Seite 16]
Seiten-Metadaten: Bilder=0, Rechtecke=4, Kurven=0, Linien=0
Observations 2/2
▪ Shadow shape can be obtained by projection
• Trivial for projection on flat surfaces
• Algorithmically very complex for projection in general case
▪ Shadow intensity
• Shadows attenuate the incoming light used in illumination model
▪ Correct shadows can only be computed with global illumination models
▪ Empirical approaches for shadow computation are widely used

10.2 Ground Plane Shadows
Static and dynamic shadow polygons
Visual Computing Group
Institute of Media Informatics
[Seite 19]
Seiten-Metadaten: Bilder=0, Rechtecke=4, Kurven=0, Linien=0
Static Shadow Polygons
▪ Render dark polygons to represent shadow regions
• Cast ray from light source through center of shadow-casting objects
• Position dark polygon where ray intersects shadow-receiving object
▪ Disadvantages
• Static shapes cannot represent geometry of dynamic scene objects
• Single intersection of ray and shadow-receiver can’t capture soft shadows
• Incorrect parts of the shadow may be drawn
Interactive Computer Graphics 09/07/2026 17
[Seite 20]
Seiten-Metadaten: Bilder=1, Rechtecke=4, Kurven=0, Linien=0
Render Static Shadow Polygons 1/2
▪ Depth value identical with thatof shadow-receiving polygon(care must be taken wrt. z-buffer
fighting)
▪ Depth value smaller than that of shadow-receiving polygon(shadow can be too large)
Interactive Computer Graphics 09/07/2026 18

Render Static Shadow Polygons 2/2
▪ Disable depth test
• Cast ray to determine shadow visibility
• Show entire shadow polygon
▪ Shadow too large and possibly in wrong places
▪ Test corners for shadow visibility
• Sufficient for planar polygons

Light Maps
▪ Static shadows can be precomputed and stored in light maps

Representation of shadows by geometry enclosing them

Shadow Volumes
▪ Shadows are considered as volume in space
▪ Originally developed by Crow in 1977
▪ Extension by Brotman and Badler in 1984
▪ Heidmann introduced the technology for efficientrendering of shadow volumes in 1991
Interactive Computer Graphics 09/07/2026 29
[Seite 32]
Seiten-Metadaten: Bilder=0, Rechtecke=4, Kurven=0, Linien=0
Initial Considerations
▪ Shadow volume shape depends on shape and positionof light source and shadow-caster
▪ All points inside shadow volume are shadowed
▪ Shadow volume generation
• Find silhouettes of shadow-casterregarding light source
• Extrudes silhouettes in light ray directionto create polygons
• Connect resulting polygons to obtain shadow volume

▪ Silhouettes edges can be found by analyzing normals
• Silhouette edge lies between front and back face (as seen from light source)
V

▪ For convex shadow-casters
L V

Shadow Volume Properties 1/2
▪ All points inside shadow volume are shadowed
▪ Shadowing can be determined for each view ray by intersection tests
• Assumption: Camera not in shadow volume
s
• At each intersection with front-face shadow polygon, intersection counter cnt is incremented
s
• At each intersection with back-face shadow polygon, intersection counter cnt is decremented
s = 0
• Positions on view rays with cnt are illuminated, all others are shadowed
▪ Only intersections before point to be rendered need to be considered

[Seite 36]
Seiten-Metadaten: Bilder=1, Rechtecke=4, Kurven=0, Linien=0
Shadow Volume Properties 2/2
Interactive Computer Graphics 09/07/2026 34
[Seite 37]
Seiten-Metadaten: Bilder=0, Rechtecke=4, Kurven=0, Linien=0
Stencil Shadow Volume
▪ Generation of shadow volumes per frame
• Works well for scenes with few moving objects
• Expensive for complex shadow volumes
• Improvement by simplifying shadow-casting geometries
▪ Four rendering passes required
• Render scene exclusively with ambient lighting
• Render front-face shadow polygons and increment stencil buffer
• Render back-face shadow polygons and decrement stencil buffer
• Render parts of scene that are not in shadow (stencil buffer equals 0)
▪ However, some details have to be considered!
Interactive Computer Graphics 09/07/2026 35
[Seite 38]
Seiten-Metadaten: Bilder=0, Rechtecke=4, Kurven=0, Linien=0
Implementation
▪ Determine visible scene objects
• Render scene without writing in color buffer
▪ Represent shadow volume in stencil buffer
• Initialize stencil buffer with 0
• Render front-face shadow polygons and increment stencil buffer by 1
• Render back-face shadow polygons and decrement stencil buffer by 1
• => Shadowed image regions are marked by >0 in stencil buffer
▪ Render shadowed parts of shadow-receiving scene objects
• Render only where stencil value >0
▪ Render non-shadowed parts of shadow-receiving scene objects
• Render only where stencil value =0

Special Case: COP in the shadows
▪ When COP lies in a shadow volume, the situation can be unclear
• Near - or far -plane can intersect shadow volume
▪ Possible solutions
s = 0
• Test COP against all shadow volumes cnt
• Clip shadow volume against view volume and perform capping
Interactive Computer Graphics 09/07/2026 37
[Seite 40]
Seiten-Metadaten: Bilder=1, Rechtecke=4, Kurven=0, Linien=0
Shadow Volume Example
Interactive Computer Graphics 09/07/2026 38
[Seite 41]
Seiten-Metadaten: Bilder=0, Rechtecke=4, Kurven=0, Linien=0
Shadow Volume Conclusions
▪ Advantages
• Shadow-casting and shadow-receiving objects can have arbitrary shapes
• Applicable for multiple light sources
• Level-of-detail adaptable through approximated geometries
• Shadow volumes for static pairs of objects and lights can be precalculated
• Self-shadowing possible
▪ Disadvantages
• Many new polygons need to be rendered
• Long thin triangles are very expensive in rasterization
• Bit depth of the stencil buffer may not be sufficient for very complex scenes (buffer overflow)
• Scene objects must be closed (no holes)

Shadow Mapping
▪ Based on z-Buffer (contains depth relative to the light source)
▪ First used within Pixar’s Renderman

Projected Shadows
▪ depth texture
▪ Rendering algorithm
• Render shadow-casting objectsas seen from the light source into depth texture
• Project depth texture using projective texturingwhen rendering shadow-receiving objects
▪ Characteristics of the process
• Works for arbitrarily shaped scene objects
• Shadow-casting and shadow-receivingscene objects can be separated
• Self-shadowing becomes possible

Pseudo Code
// generate shadow map w.r.t light source
generateShadowMap();
// render scene from COP
for all rasterized fragments do {
Transform fragment xyz into lights coordinate system
A = depthmap(x,y)
B = z-value of fragments xyz
if (A < B)
fragment is shadowed
else
fragment is lit
}
}

Properties
▪ Shadow maps are static when scene and lighting are static
▪ Shadow quality depends on shadow map resolution
▪ Shadow mapping has three main problems
• View volume problem
• Bias problem
• Aliasing problem
Interactive Computer Graphics 09/07/2026 46
[Seite 50]
Seiten-Metadaten: Bilder=3, Rechtecke=4, Kurven=0, Linien=0
View Volume Problem
▪ When vertex lies outside light source’s view volume,required depth information is missing
▪ Possible remedies
• Use cubic shadow map (similar to cubic environment map)
• Use only spotlights

Chapter Summary

Seiten-Metadaten: Bilder=0, Rechtecke=4, Kurven=0, Linien=0
▪ Shadows in Visual Perception
• Enhance depth perception and object relationships
• Create appealing visual effects and atmosphere
▪ Shadow Definitions and Types
• Shadow-casting (Occluder) vs. shadow-receiving (Receiver) objects
• Self-shadowing: Same object casts and receives shadow
• Hard shadows (umbra) from point lights, soft shadows (penumbra) from area lights
▪ Shadow Calculation Methods
• Techniques include ground plane shadows, light maps, shadow volumes, and shadow maps
• Ground Plane Shadows
• Static and dynamic shadow polygons
• Challenges with representing dynamic scenes and soft shadows
▪ Light Maps
• Precomputed static shadows with interpolation for soft shadows
▪ Shadow Volumes
• Geometrically enclosed shadows

Zip-Datei: opengl-rotatingcube/CMakeLists.txt
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.20)
project(RotatingCube LANGUAGES C CXX)

set(CMAKE_C_STANDARD 11)
set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 17)

include(FetchContent)

FetchContent_Declare(
    glfw
    GIT_REPOSITORY https://github.com/glfw/glfw.git
    GIT_TAG 3.4
)
FetchContent_MakeAvailable(glfw)

add_executable(RotatingCube
    src/main.cpp
    external/glad/src/glad.c
)

target_include_directories(RotatingCube PRIVATE
    external/glad/include
)

target_link_libraries(RotatingCube PRIVATE glfw)

if (WIN32)
    target_link_libraries(RotatingCube PRIVATE opengl32)
elseif (APPLE)
    target_link_libraries(RotatingCube PRIVATE "-framework OpenGL")
else()
    find_package(OpenGL REQUIRED)
    target_link_libraries(RotatingCube PRIVATE OpenGL::GL)
endif()

 * See the Implementer's Guidelines for information about where this file
 * should be located on your system and for more details of its use:
 *    http://www.khronos.org/registry/implementers_guide.pdf
 *
 * This file should be included as
 *        #include <KHR/khrplatform.h>
 * by Khronos client API header files that use its types and defines.
 *
 * The types in khrplatform.h should only be used to define API-specific types.
 *
 * Types defined in khrplatform.h:
 *    khronos_int8_t              signed   8  bit
 *    khronos_uint8_t             unsigned 8  bit
 *    khronos_int16_t             signed   16 bit
 *    khronos_uint16_t            unsigned 16 bit
 *    khronos_int32_t             signed   32 bit
 *    khronos_uint32_t            unsigned 32 bit
 *    khronos_int64_t             signed   64 bit
 *    khronos_uint64_t            unsigned 64 bit
 *    khronos_intptr_t            signed   same number of bits as a pointer
 *    khronos_uintptr_t           unsigned same number of bits as a pointer
 *    khronos_ssize_t             signed   size
 *    khronos_usize_t             unsigned size
 *    khronos_float_t             signed   32 bit floating point
 *    khronos_time_ns_t           unsigned 64 bit time in nanoseconds
 *    khronos_utime_nanoseconds_t unsigned time interval or absolute time in
 *                                         nanoseconds
 *    khronos_stime_nanoseconds_t signed time interval in nanoseconds
 *    khronos_boolean_enum_t      enumerated boolean type. This should
 *      only be used as a base type when a client API's boolean type is
 *      an enum. Client APIs which use an integer or other type for
 *      booleans cannot use this as the base type for their boolean.
 *
 * Tokens defined in khrplatform.h:
 *
 *    KHRONOS_FALSE, KHRONOS_TRUE Enumerated boolean false/true values.
 *
 *    KHRONOS_SUPPORT_INT64 is 1 if 64 bit integers are supported; otherwise 0.
 *    KHRONOS_SUPPORT_FLOAT is 1 if floats are supported; otherwise 0.
 *
 * Calling convention macros defined in this file:
 *    KHRONOS_APICALL
 *    KHRONOS_APIENTRY
 *    KHRONOS_APIATTRIBUTES
 *
 * These may be used in function prototypes as:
 *
 *      KHRONOS_APICALL void KHRONOS_APIENTRY funcname(
 *                                  int arg1,
 *                                  int arg2) KHRONOS_APIATTRIBUTES;
 */

#endif

/*-------------------------------------------------------------------------

 *-----------------------------------------------------------------------*/
#if (defined(__STDC_VERSION__) && __STDC_VERSION__ >= 199901L) || defined(__GNUC__) || defined(__SCO__) || defined(__USLC__)


/*
 * Using <stdint.h>
 */
#include <stdint.h>
typedef int32_t                 khronos_int32_t;
typedef uint32_t                khronos_uint32_t;
typedef int64_t                 khronos_int64_t;
typedef uint64_t                khronos_uint64_t;
#define KHRONOS_SUPPORT_INT64   1
#define KHRONOS_SUPPORT_FLOAT   1
/*
 * To support platform where unsigned long cannot be used interchangeably with
 * inptr_t (e.g. CHERI-extended ISAs), we can use the stdint.h intptr_t.
 * Ideally, we could just use (u)intptr_t everywhere, but this could result in
 * ABI breakage if khronos_uintptr_t is changed from unsigned long to
 * unsigned long long or similar (this results in different C++ name mangling).
 * To avoid changes for existing platforms, we restrict usage of intptr_t to
 * platforms where the size of a pointer is larger than the size of long.
 */
#if defined(__SIZEOF_LONG__) && defined(__SIZEOF_POINTER__)
#if __SIZEOF_POINTER__ > __SIZEOF_LONG__
#define KHRONOS_USE_INTPTR_T
#endif
#endif

#elif defined(__VMS ) || defined(__sgi)

/*
 * Using <inttypes.h>
 */
#include <inttypes.h>
typedef int32_t                 khronos_int32_t;
typedef uint32_t                khronos_uint32_t;
typedef int64_t                 khronos_int64_t;
typedef uint64_t                khronos_uint64_t;
#define KHRONOS_SUPPORT_INT64   1
#define KHRONOS_SUPPORT_FLOAT   1

#elif defined(_WIN32) && !defined(__SCITECH_SNAP__)

/*
 * Win32
 */
typedef __int32                 khronos_int32_t;
typedef unsigned __int32        khronos_uint32_t;
typedef __int64                 khronos_int64_t;
typedef unsigned __int64        khronos_uint64_t;
#define KHRONOS_SUPPORT_INT64   1
#define KHRONOS_SUPPORT_FLOAT   1

#elif defined(__sun__) || defined(__digital__)

/*
 * Sun or Digital
 */
typedef int                     khronos_int32_t;
typedef unsigned int            khronos_uint32_t;
#if defined(__arch64__) || defined(_LP64)
typedef long int                khronos_int64_t;
typedef unsigned long int       khronos_uint64_t;
#else
typedef long long int           khronos_int64_t;
typedef unsigned long long int  khronos_uint64_t;
#endif /* __arch64__ */
#define KHRONOS_SUPPORT_INT64   1
#define KHRONOS_SUPPORT_FLOAT   1

#elif 0

/*
 * Hypothetical platform with no float or int64 support
 */
typedef int                     khronos_int32_t;
typedef unsigned int            khronos_uint32_t;
#define KHRONOS_SUPPORT_INT64   0
#define KHRONOS_SUPPORT_FLOAT   0

#else

/*
 * Generic fallback
 */
#include <stdint.h>
typedef int32_t                 khronos_int32_t;
typedef uint32_t                khronos_uint32_t;
typedef int64_t                 khronos_int64_t;
typedef uint64_t                khronos_uint64_t;
#define KHRONOS_SUPPORT_INT64   1
#define KHRONOS_SUPPORT_FLOAT   1

#endif


/*
 * Types that are (so far) the same on all platforms
 */
typedef signed   char          khronos_int8_t;
typedef unsigned char          khronos_uint8_t;
typedef signed   short int     khronos_int16_t;
typedef unsigned short int     khronos_uint16_t;

/*
 * Types that differ between LLP64 and LP64 architectures - in LLP64,
 * pointers are 64 bits, but 'long' is still 32 bits. Win64 appears
 * to be the only LLP64 architecture in current use.
 */
#ifdef KHRONOS_USE_INTPTR_T
typedef intptr_t               khronos_intptr_t;
typedef uintptr_t              khronos_uintptr_t;
#elif defined(_WIN64)
typedef signed   long long int khronos_intptr_t;
typedef unsigned long long int khronos_uintptr_t;
#else
typedef signed   long  int     khronos_intptr_t;
typedef unsigned long  int     khronos_uintptr_t;
#endif

#if defined(_WIN64)
typedef signed   long long int khronos_ssize_t;
typedef unsigned long long int khronos_usize_t;
#else
typedef signed   long  int     khronos_ssize_t;
typedef unsigned long  int     khronos_usize_t;
#endif

#if KHRONOS_SUPPORT_FLOAT
/*
 * Float type
 */
typedef          float         khronos_float_t;
#endif

#if KHRONOS_SUPPORT_INT64
/* Time types
 *
 * These types can be used to represent a time interval in nanoseconds or
 * an absolute Unadjusted System Time.  Unadjusted System Time is the number
 * of nanoseconds since some arbitrary system event (e.g. since the last
 * time the system booted).  The Unadjusted System Time is an unsigned
 * 64 bit value that wraps back to 0 every 584 years.  Time intervals
 * may be either signed or unsigned.
 */
typedef khronos_uint64_t       khronos_utime_nanoseconds_t;
typedef khronos_int64_t        khronos_stime_nanoseconds_t;
#endif

/*
 * Dummy value used to pad enum types to 32 bits.
 */
#ifndef KHRONOS_MAX_ENUM
#define KHRONOS_MAX_ENUM 0x7FFFFFFF
#endif

/*
 * Enumerated boolean type
 *
 * Values other than zero should be considered to be true.  Therefore
 * comparisons should not be made against KHRONOS_TRUE.
 */
typedef enum {
    KHRONOS_FALSE = 0,
    KHRONOS_TRUE  = 1,
    KHRONOS_BOOLEAN_ENUM_FORCE_SIZE = KHRONOS_MAX_ENUM
} khronos_boolean_enum_t;

#endif /* __khrplatform_h_ */

            }

#endif
    return 1;
}

static int has_ext(const char *ext) {
#ifdef _GLAD_IS_SOME_NEW_VERSION
    if(max_loaded_major < 3) {
#endif
        const char *extensions;
        const char *loc;
        const char *terminator;
        extensions = exts;
        if(extensions == NULL || ext == NULL) {
            return 0;
        }

        while(1) {
            loc = strstr(extensions, ext);
            if(loc == NULL) {
                return 0;
            }

            terminator = loc + strlen(ext);
            if((loc == extensions || *(loc - 1) == ' ') &&
                (*terminator == ' ' || *terminator == '\0')) {
                return 1;
            }
            extensions = terminator;
        }
#ifdef _GLAD_IS_SOME_NEW_VERSION

                return 1;
            }
        }
    }
#endif

    return 0;

static int find_extensionsGL(void) {
	if (!get_exts()) return 0;
	(void)&has_ext;
	free_exts();
	return 1;
}

static void find_coreGL(void) {

    /* Thank you @elmindreda
     * https://github.com/elmindreda/greg/blob/master/templates/greg.c.in#L176
     * https://github.com/glfw/glfw/blob/master/src/context.c#L36
     */
    int i, major, minor;

    const char* version;
    const char* prefixes[] = {
        "OpenGL ES-CM ",
        "OpenGL ES-CL ",
        "OpenGL ES ",
        NULL
    };

    version = (const char*) glGetString(GL_VERSION);
    if (!version) return;

    for (i = 0;  prefixes[i];  i++) {
        const size_t length = strlen(prefixes[i]);
        if (strncmp(version, prefixes[i], length) == 0) {
            version += length;
            break;
        }
    }

/* PR #18 */
#ifdef _MSC_VER
    sscanf_s(version, "%d.%d", &major, &minor);
#else
    sscanf(version, "%d.%d", &major, &minor);
#endif

    GLVersion.major = major; GLVersion.minor = minor;
    max_loaded_major = major; max_loaded_minor = minor;
	GLAD_GL_VERSION_1_0 = (major == 1 && minor >= 0) || major > 1;
	GLAD_GL_VERSION_1_1 = (major == 1 && minor >= 1) || major > 1;
	GLAD_GL_VERSION_1_2 = (major == 1 && minor >= 2) || major > 1;
	GLAD_GL_VERSION_1_3 = (major == 1 && minor >= 3) || major > 1;
	GLAD_GL_VERSION_1_4 = (major == 1 && minor >= 4) || major > 1;
	GLAD_GL_VERSION_1_5 = (major == 1 && minor >= 5) || major > 1;
	GLAD_GL_VERSION_2_0 = (major == 2 && minor >= 0) || major > 2;
	GLAD_GL_VERSION_2_1 = (major == 2 && minor >= 1) || major > 2;
	GLAD_GL_VERSION_3_0 = (major == 3 && minor >= 0) || major > 3;
	GLAD_GL_VERSION_3_1 = (major == 3 && minor >= 1) || major > 3;
	GLAD_GL_VERSION_3_2 = (major == 3 && minor >= 2) || major > 3;
	GLAD_GL_VERSION_3_3 = (major == 3 && minor >= 3) || major > 3;
	if (GLVersion.major > 3 || (GLVersion.major >= 3 && GLVersion.minor >= 3)) {
		max_loaded_major = 3;
		max_loaded_minor = 3;
	}
}

int gladLoadGLLoader(GLADloadproc load) {
	GLVersion.major = 0; GLVersion.minor = 0;
	glGetString = (PFNGLGETSTRINGPROC)load("glGetString");
	if(glGetString == NULL) return 0;
	if(glGetString(GL_VERSION) == NULL) return 0;
	find_coreGL();
	load_GL_VERSION_1_0(load);
	load_GL_VERSION_1_1(load);
	load_GL_VERSION_1_2(load);
	load_GL_VERSION_1_3(load);
	load_GL_VERSION_1_4(load);
	load_GL_VERSION_1_5(load);
	load_GL_VERSION_2_0(load);
	load_GL_VERSION_2_1(load);
	load_GL_VERSION_3_0(load);
	load_GL_VERSION_3_1(load);
	load_GL_VERSION_3_2(load);
	load_GL_VERSION_3_3(load);

	if (!find_extensionsGL()) return 0;
	return GLVersion.major != 0 || GLVersion.minor != 0;
}

#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <math.h>

#include <glad/glad.h>
#include <GLFW/glfw3.h>

static GLuint vao = 0;
static GLuint vbo = 0;
static GLuint program = 0;
static GLint u_mvp_location = -1;

static void error_callback(int error, const char* description) {
    (void)error;
    fputs(description, stderr);
    fputc('\n', stderr);
}

static void framebuffer_size_callback(GLFWwindow* window, int width, int height) {
    (void)window;
    glViewport(0, 0, width, height);
}

static void key_callback(GLFWwindow* window, int key, int scancode, int action, int mods) {
    (void)scancode;
    (void)mods;

    if (key == GLFW_KEY_ESCAPE && action == GLFW_PRESS)
        glfwSetWindowShouldClose(window, GLFW_TRUE);
}

static GLuint compile_shader(GLenum type, const char* src) {
    GLuint shader = glCreateShader(type);
    glShaderSource(shader, 1, &src, NULL);
    glCompileShader(shader);

    GLint ok = 0;
    glGetShaderiv(shader, GL_COMPILE_STATUS, &ok);
    if (!ok) {
        char log[1024];
        glGetShaderInfoLog(shader, sizeof(log), NULL, log);
        fprintf(stderr, "Shader compile error:\n%s\n", log);
        glDeleteShader(shader);
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }

    return shader;
}

static GLuint create_program(const char* vs_src, const char* fs_src) {
    GLuint vs = compile_shader(GL_VERTEX_SHADER, vs_src);
    GLuint fs = compile_shader(GL_FRAGMENT_SHADER, fs_src);

    GLuint prog = glCreateProgram();
    glAttachShader(prog, vs);
    glAttachShader(prog, fs);
    glLinkProgram(prog);

    glDeleteShader(vs);
    glDeleteShader(fs);

    GLint ok = 0;
    glGetProgramiv(prog, GL_LINK_STATUS, &ok);
    if (!ok) {
        char log[1024];
        glGetProgramInfoLog(prog, sizeof(log), NULL, log);
        fprintf(stderr, "Program link error:\n%s\n", log);
        glDeleteProgram(prog);
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }

    return prog;
}

static void mat4_identity(float m[16]) {
    for (int i = 0; i < 16; ++i)
        m[i] = 0.0f;

    m[0] = 1.0f;
    m[5] = 1.0f;
    m[10] = 1.0f;
    m[15] = 1.0f;
}

static void mat4_multiply(float out[16], const float a[16], const float b[16]) {
    float r[16];

    for (int col = 0; col < 4; ++col) {
        for (int row = 0; row < 4; ++row) {
            r[col * 4 + row] =
                a[0 * 4 + row] * b[col * 4 + 0] +
                a[1 * 4 + row] * b[col * 4 + 1] +
                a[2 * 4 + row] * b[col * 4 + 2] +
                a[3 * 4 + row] * b[col * 4 + 3];
        }
    }

    for (int i = 0; i < 16; ++i)
        out[i] = r[i];
}

static void mat4_translate(float m[16], float x, float y, float z) {
    mat4_identity(m);
    m[12] = x;
    m[13] = y;
    m[14] = z;
}

static void mat4_rotate_x(float m[16], float angle) {
    float c = cosf(angle);
    float s = sinf(angle);

    mat4_identity(m);
    m[5] = c;
    m[6] = s;
    m[9] = -s;
    m[10] = c;
}

static void mat4_rotate_y(float m[16], float angle) {
    float c = cosf(angle);
    float s = sinf(angle);

    mat4_identity(m);
    m[0] = c;
    m[2] = -s;
    m[8] = s;
    m[10] = c;
}

static void mat4_perspective(float m[16], float fovy_radians, float aspect, float z_near, float z_far) {
    float f = 1.0f / tanf(fovy_radians * 0.5f);

    for (int i = 0; i < 16; ++i)
        m[i] = 0.0f;

    m[0] = f / aspect;
    m[5] = f;
    m[10] = (z_far + z_near) / (z_near - z_far);
    m[11] = -1.0f;
    m[14] = (2.0f * z_far * z_near) / (z_near - z_far);
}

static void init_render_scene(void) {
    static const GLfloat vertices[] = {
        /* positions          colors */

        /* front - red */
        -0.5f, -0.5f,  0.5f,  1.0f, 0.0f, 0.0f,
         0.5f, -0.5f,  0.5f,  1.0f, 0.0f, 0.0f,
         0.5f,  0.5f,  0.5f,  1.0f, 0.0f, 0.0f,
        -0.5f, -0.5f,  0.5f,  1.0f, 0.0f, 0.0f,
         0.5f,  0.5f,  0.5f,  1.0f, 0.0f, 0.0f,
        -0.5f,  0.5f,  0.5f,  1.0f, 0.0f, 0.0f,

        /* back - green */
        -0.5f, -0.5f, -0.5f,  0.0f, 1.0f, 0.0f,
        -0.5f,  0.5f, -0.5f,  0.0f, 1.0f, 0.0f,
         0.5f,  0.5f, -0.5f,  0.0f, 1.0f, 0.0f,
        -0.5f, -0.5f, -0.5f,  0.0f, 1.0f, 0.0f,
         0.5f,  0.5f, -0.5f,  0.0f, 1.0f, 0.0f,
         0.5f, -0.5f, -0.5f,  0.0f, 1.0f, 0.0f,

        /* left - blue */
        -0.5f, -0.5f, -0.5f,  0.0f, 0.0f, 1.0f,
        -0.5f, -0.5f,  0.5f,  0.0f, 0.0f, 1.0f,
        -0.5f,  0.5f,  0.5f,  0.0f, 0.0f, 1.0f,
        -0.5f, -0.5f, -0.5f,  0.0f, 0.0f, 1.0f,
        -0.5f,  0.5f,  0.5f,  0.0f, 0.0f, 1.0f,
        -0.5f,  0.5f, -0.5f,  0.0f, 0.0f, 1.0f,

        /* right - yellow */
         0.5f, -0.5f, -0.5f,  1.0f, 1.0f, 0.0f,
         0.5f,  0.5f, -0.5f,  1.0f, 1.0f, 0.0f,
         0.5f,  0.5f,  0.5f,  1.0f, 1.0f, 0.0f,
         0.5f, -0.5f, -0.5f,  1.0f, 1.0f, 0.0f,
         0.5f,  0.5f,  0.5f,  1.0f, 1.0f, 0.0f,
         0.5f, -0.5f,  0.5f,  1.0f, 1.0f, 0.0f,

        /* top - magenta */
        -0.5f,  0.5f, -0.5f,  1.0f, 0.0f, 1.0f,
        -0.5f,  0.5f,  0.5f,  1.0f, 0.0f, 1.0f,
         0.5f,  0.5f,  0.5f,  1.0f, 0.0f, 1.0f,
        -0.5f,  0.5f, -0.5f,  1.0f, 0.0f, 1.0f,
         0.5f,  0.5f,  0.5f,  1.0f, 0.0f, 1.0f,
         0.5f,  0.5f, -0.5f,  1.0f, 0.0f, 1.0f,

        /* bottom - cyan */
        -0.5f, -0.5f, -0.5f,  0.0f, 1.0f, 1.0f,
         0.5f, -0.5f, -0.5f,  0.0f, 1.0f, 1.0f,
         0.5f, -0.5f,  0.5f,  0.0f, 1.0f, 1.0f,
        -0.5f, -0.5f, -0.5f,  0.0f, 1.0f, 1.0f,
         0.5f, -0.5f,  0.5f,  0.0f, 1.0f, 1.0f,
        -0.5f, -0.5f,  0.5f,  0.0f, 1.0f, 1.0f
    };

    static const char* vs_src =
        "#version 330 core\n"
        "layout (location = 0) in vec3 aPos;\n"
        "layout (location = 1) in vec3 aColor;\n"
        "uniform mat4 uMVP;\n"
        "out vec3 vColor;\n"
        "void main(void) {\n"
        "    gl_Position = uMVP * vec4(aPos, 1.0);\n"
        "    vColor = aColor;\n"
        "}\n";

    static const char* fs_src =
        "#version 330 core\n"
        "in vec3 vColor;\n"
        "out vec4 FragColor;\n"
        "void main(void) {\n"
        "    FragColor = vec4(vColor, 1.0);\n"
        "}\n";

    program = create_program(vs_src, fs_src);
    u_mvp_location = glGetUniformLocation(program, "uMVP");

    glGenVertexArrays(1, &vao);
    glGenBuffers(1, &vbo);

    glBindVertexArray(vao);

    glBindBuffer(GL_ARRAY_BUFFER, vbo);
    glBufferData(GL_ARRAY_BUFFER, sizeof(vertices), vertices, GL_STATIC_DRAW);

    glVertexAttribPointer(0, 3, GL_FLOAT, GL_FALSE, 6 * sizeof(GLfloat), (void*)0);
    glEnableVertexAttribArray(0);

    glVertexAttribPointer(1, 3, GL_FLOAT, GL_FALSE, 6 * sizeof(GLfloat), (void*)(3 * sizeof(GLfloat)));
    glEnableVertexAttribArray(1);

    glBindBuffer(GL_ARRAY_BUFFER, 0);
    glBindVertexArray(0);

    glEnable(GL_DEPTH_TEST);
}

static void render_scene(GLFWwindow* window) {
    int width, height;
    glfwGetFramebufferSize(window, &width, &height);

    if (height == 0)
        height = 1;

    float aspect = (float)width / (float)height;
    float time = (float)glfwGetTime();

    float proj[16];
    float view[16];
    float rot_x[16];
    float rot_y[16];
    float model[16];
    float temp[16];
    float vp[16];
    float mvp[16];

    mat4_perspective(proj, 45.0f * 3.1415926535f / 180.0f, aspect, 0.1f, 100.0f);
    mat4_translate(view, 0.0f, 0.0f, -3.0f);
    mat4_rotate_y(rot_y, time);
    mat4_rotate_x(rot_x, time * 0.7f);

    mat4_multiply(model, rot_y, rot_x);
    mat4_multiply(vp, proj, view);
    mat4_multiply(mvp, vp, model);

    glClear(GL_COLOR_BUFFER_BIT | GL_DEPTH_BUFFER_BIT);

    glUseProgram(program);
    glUniformMatrix4fv(u_mvp_location, 1, GL_FALSE, mvp);

    glBindVertexArray(vao);
    glDrawArrays(GL_TRIANGLES, 0, 36);
    glBindVertexArray(0);
}

static void cleanup_render_scene(void) {
    if (vbo)     glDeleteBuffers(1, &vbo);
    if (vao)     glDeleteVertexArrays(1, &vao);
    if (program) glDeleteProgram(program);
}

int main(void) {
    GLFWwindow* window;

    glfwSetErrorCallback(error_callback);

    if (!glfwInit())
        return EXIT_FAILURE;

    glfwWindowHint(GLFW_CONTEXT_VERSION_MAJOR, 3);
    glfwWindowHint(GLFW_CONTEXT_VERSION_MINOR, 3);
    glfwWindowHint(GLFW_OPENGL_PROFILE, GLFW_OPENGL_CORE_PROFILE);
#ifdef __APPLE__
    glfwWindowHint(GLFW_OPENGL_FORWARD_COMPAT, GL_TRUE);
#endif

    window = glfwCreateWindow(640, 480, "Rotating Cube", NULL, NULL);
    if (!window) {
        glfwTerminate();
        return EXIT_FAILURE;
    }

    glfwMakeContextCurrent(window);
    glfwSetKeyCallback(window, key_callback);
    glfwSetFramebufferSizeCallback(window, framebuffer_size_callback);

    if (!gladLoadGLLoader((GLADloadproc)glfwGetProcAddress)) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Failed to initialize GLAD\n");
        glfwDestroyWindow(window);
        glfwTerminate();
        return EXIT_FAILURE;
    }

    glViewport(0, 0, 640, 480);
    glClearColor(0.1f, 0.1f, 0.15f, 1.0f);

    init_render_scene();

    while (!glfwWindowShouldClose(window)) {
        render_scene(window);
        glfwSwapBuffers(window);
        glfwPollEvents();
    }

    cleanup_render_scene();
    glfwDestroyWindow(window);
    glfwTerminate();
    return EXIT_SUCCESS;
}

  -  Now that the geometry has been transformed to its representation on the
  - screen, parts outside screen must be clipped away
  - (cid:127) Clipping ensures that following costly computations
  - (e.g., rasterization, illumination, shading) are only applied to visible parts
  -  Since clipping is performed for all geometry, algorithms are highly optimized
  - Clipping Projected Geometry 2/2
  -  Analytical clipping
  - (cid:127) Clipping before raster conversion, clipped primitives are raster-converted
  - (cid:127) Compute time savings if clipped primitive is much smaller than unclipped
  - (cid:127) OpenGL: clipping against canonical view volume
  -  Pixel-based clipping
  - (cid:127) Clipping during or after raster conversion
  - (cid:127) Only pixels in the clip region are used

  - (cid:127) Given scene objects and virtual camera
  - (cid:127) Determine visible parts of scene objects

/* block.invisible vs .invisible
 * block.hidden vs .invisible
 *
 * uses .invisible where the rest of Moodle uses @mixin dimmed
 * fixible in block renderer?
 *
 * There's seems to be even more naming confusion here since,
 * blocks can be actually 'visible' (or not) to students,
 * marked 'visible' but really just dimmed to indicate to editors
 * that students can't see them or  'visible' to the user who
 * collapses them, 'visible' if you have the right role and in
 * different circumstances different sections of a block can
 * be 'visible' or not.
 *
 * currently worked around in renderers.php function block{}
 * by rewriting the class name "invisible" to "dimmed",
 * though the blocks don't look particularly different apart
 * from their contents disappearing. Maybe try .muted? or
 * dimming all the edit icons apart from unhide, might be a
 * nice effect, though they'd still be active. Maybe reverse
 * it to white?
 */
.section.hidden,
.block.hidden,
.block.invisible {
  visibility: visible;
  display: block;
}

/* .row vs .row
 *
 * very tricky to track down this when it goes wrong,
 * since the styles are applied to generated content
 *
 * basically if you see things shifted left or right compared
 * with where they should be check for a .row
 */
.forumpost .row {
  margin-left: 0 !important; /* stylelint-disable-line declaration-no-important */
}

.forumpost .row:before,
.forumpost .row:after {
  content: none;
}

/* fieldset.hidden vs .hidden
 *
 * Moodle uses fieldset.hidden for mforms, to signify a collection of
 * form elements that don't have a box drawn round them. Bootstrap
 * uses hidden for stuff that is hidden in various responsive modes.
 *
 * Relatedly, there is also fieldset.invisiblefieldset which hides the
 * border and sets the display to inline.
 *
 * Originally this just set block and visible, but it is used
 * in random question dialogue in Quiz,
 * that dialogue is hidden and shown, so when hidden the
 * above workaround leaves you with a button floating around
 */
fieldset.hidden {
  display: inherit;
  visibility: inherit;
}

/* .container vs .container
 *
 * bootstrap uses .container to set the width of the layout at 960px or so, Moodle uses it
 * in the Quiz to contain the questions to add. If you don't overule the Bootstrap code,
 * it becomes near unuseable.
 */
#questionbank + .container {
  width: auto;
}
